cases.title: Mustang Panda Recent Activity: Dll-Sideloading trojans with temporal C2 servers

candidates.title: Mustang Panda PlugX DLL Sideloading Campaign (June 2020)
candidates.description: A malware sample uses DLL sideloading with a legitimate Adobe Swite binary to load a PlugX Trojan. The installer drops files, the loader decrypts and executes the final payload, and the malware communicates with C2 servers that resolve only during specific hours.

actions.name: Download installer
actions.description: The sample is downloaded from a URL.

evidence.quote: The sample in question is downloaded from the following link “http://miandfish.]store/player/install\_flash\_player.exe”
The sample in question is downloaded from the following link “http://miandfish.]store/player/install\_flash\_player.exe”

actions.name: Drop files
actions.description: The installer drops a legitimate binary, a malicious DLL, and an encrypted PlugX file into a folder.

contexts.name: legitimate binary vulnerable to dll sideload

evidence.quote: the legitimate binary vulnerable to dll sideload

contexts.name: small dll that acts as a loader

evidence.quote: the small dll that acts as a loader for the final threat
the binary file, which consists of the encrypted PlugX sample
drops in the folder “C:\ProgramData\AAM Updatesnnk”

The binary consists of an installer, which drops in the folder “C:\ProgramData\AAM Updatesnnk” the legitimate binary vulnerable to dll sideload, the small dll that acts as a loader for the final threat, and the binary file, which consists of the encrypted PlugX sample.

actions.name: Execute legitimate binary
actions.description: The installer runs the legitimate binary, causing the PlugX threat to be loaded.

evidence.quote: After deploying the three files, the installer runs the legitimate binary, causing the final PlugX threat to be loaded by it.

actions.name: Load malicious DLL
actions.description: The legitimate Adobe Swite binary loads the malicious hex.dll via DLL sideloading.

evidence.quote: the legitimate vulnerable binary is part of Adobe’s Swite which will load any library named “hex.dll” that is next to the executable
the legitimate vulnerable binary is part of Adobe’s Swite which will load any library named “hex.dll” that is next to the executable

actions.name: Decrypt and load PlugX
actions.description: The hex.dll loader decrypts the .dat file using a hardcoded XOR key and loads the PlugX payload into memory.

evidence.quote: checks the existence of the .dat file which is hardcoded (adobeupdate.dat in this case)

the Main function of the library, on the other hand, calls a function that checks the existence of the .dat file which is hardcoded (adobeupdate.dat in this case), loads it, extracts the first string of the binary and uses it as XOR key to decode the rest of the file, which consists on the final threat.

actions.name: Execute PlugX in memory
actions.description: The loader makes the decrypted PlugX executable and launches its logic from byte 0.

evidence.quote: When it finishes deciphering it, it loads the malware into memory, makes a “Memprotect” to make it executable and launches its logic from the byte 0 of the binary.

actions.name: Decrypt configuration
actions.description: PlugX decrypts its own configuration from the .data section using the hardcoded key '123456789'.

evidence.quote: After loading the IAT and leaving everything ready as a normal executable, this threat decrypts its own config, which is encrypted in XOR in the .data section of the binary.
This time the decryption key is hardcoded in the binary, and is the string “123456789”.

actions.name: Communicate with C2 servers
actions.description: PlugX uses domains as C2 servers that resolve to an IP only during specific hours.

evidence.quote: This particular sample has the domains “www.destroy2013.]com” and “www.fitehook.]com” as c2 servers
This particular sample has the domains “www.destroy2013.]com” and “www.fitehook.]com” as c2 servers
from 1-3 AM (UTC) to 8-9 AM (UTC) it resolves to the IP “107.150.112.]250

This particular sample has the domains “www.destroy2013.]com” and “www.fitehook.]com” as c2 servers, and we have seen that they have a very characteristic behavior, since most of the day they resolve to 127.0.0.1, but from 1-3 AM (UTC) to 8-9 AM (UTC) it resolves to the IP “107.150.112.]250, except for weekends that it resolves constantly to 127.0.0.1

The binary consists of an installer, which drops in the folder “C:\ProgramData\AAM Updatesnnk” the legitimate binary vulnerable to dll sideload, the small dll that acts as a loader for the final threat, and the binary file, which consists of the encrypted PlugX sample.
After deploying the three files, the installer runs the legitimate binary, causing the final PlugX threat to be loaded by it.
the legitimate vulnerable binary is part of Adobe’s Swite which will load any library named “hex.dll” that is next to the executable

the Main function of the library, on the other hand, calls a function that checks the existence of the .dat file which is hardcoded (adobeupdate.dat in this case), loads it, extracts the first string of the binary and uses it as XOR key to decode the rest of the file, which consists on the final threat.
When it finishes deciphering it, it loads the malware into memory, makes a “Memprotect” to make it executable and launches its logic from the byte 0 of the binary.
After loading the IAT and leaving everything ready as a normal executable, this threat decrypts its own config, which is encrypted in XOR in the .data section of the binary.

After decrypting its configuration, it contains the folder where the binary must be installed, a XOR key that will use to encrypt it’s traffic and a list of up to 4 domains or IP addresses of command and control servers together with the port to be used.
it has been possible to verify how both the loader and the final threat coincide in a high percentage with the samples of the “Mustang Panda” group

cases.title: Squirrelwaffle: New Loader Delivering Cobalt Strike

candidates.title: Squirrelwaffle Campaign via Word Documents
candidates.description: Squirrelwaffle loader delivered via malicious Word documents with macros, leading to Cobalt Strike deployment.

actions.name: Send spam emails with malicious URLs
actions.description: The campaign starts with spam emails using email thread hijacking to deliver URLs that download a ZIP containing a malicious Word document.

evidence.quote: Squirrelwaffle campaigns generally start via spam emails that attempt to convince victims to click an embedded URL using a technique known as email thread hijacking.
Squirrelwaffle campaigns generally start via spam emails that attempt to convince victims to click an embedded URL using a technique known as email thread hijacking.

actions.name: Download ZIP with malicious document
actions.description: Victim clicks the URL and downloads a ZIP file containing a Microsoft Word document.

evidence.quote: Once a victim clicks on the URL, a ZIP file is downloaded that contains a Microsoft Word document.
Once a victim clicks on the URL, a ZIP file is downloaded that contains a Microsoft Word document.

actions.name: Enable macro in Word document
actions.description: User enables macro in the Word document, which uses a DocuSign template lure.

evidence.quote: This document is using a DocuSign template lure that instructs the user to enable a macro to view the content
This document is using a DocuSign template lure that instructs the user to enable a macro to view the content

actions.name: Execute malicious VBA macro
actions.description: AutoOpen() subroutine calls efile() in bxh module, which extracts and executes embedded VBS file.

evidence.quote: There is a UserForm object in the document which contains a VBS file named pin.vbs that is embedded in the caption of the DocuSign image.
The document that contains the macro code leverages cscript.exe to extract the embedded VBS file, which is written to the %ProgramData% folder, and executed using wscript.exe.
The document that contains the macro code leverages cscript.exe to extract the embedded VBS file, which is written to the %ProgramData% folder, and executed using wscript.exe.
Once the user enables the macro, an *AutoOpen()* subroutine is called which then executes a malicious Visual Basic Application (VBA) macro.
Here, the *AutoOpen()* subroutine calls another function *efile*() in the *bxh* module.
The document that contains the macro code leverages cscript.exe to extract the embedded VBS file, which is written to the %ProgramData% folder, and executed using wscript.exe.

actions.name: Download Squirrelwaffle loader via VBS
actions.description: VBS file contains obfuscated PowerShell script with 5 URLs to download Squirrelwaffle payload as ww1.dll.

evidence.quote: The payload is written to %ProgramData% with the filename ww1.dll.
hxxps://priyacareers[.]com/u9hDQN9Yy7g/pt.html
hxxps://perfectdemos[.]com/Gv1iNAuMKZ/pt.html
hxxps://bussiness-z[.]ml/ze8pCNTIkrIS/pt.html
hxxps://cablingpoint[.]com/ByH5NDoE3kQA/pt.html
hxxps://bonus.corporatebusinessmachines[.]co.in/1Y0qVNce/pt.html
This VBS file contains an obfuscated PowerShell script with 5 different URLs to download the Squirrelwaffle payload as shown in Figure 3.
The payload is written to %ProgramData% with the filename ww1.dll.

actions.name: Execute Squirrelwaffle loader
actions.description: Payload DLL executed via rundll32.exe by invoking export function ldr.

evidence.quote: The payload DLL is executed via rundll32.exe by invoking the export function name *ldr*.
The payload DLL is executed via rundll32.exe by invoking the export function name *ldr*.

actions.name: Communicate with C2 server
actions.description: Squirrelwaffle sends HTTP POST with encrypted system info to C2 and receives response possibly containing second-stage payload.

evidence.quote: Host: test.dirigu.ro
The CnC communication protocol utilizes an HTTP POST request with a Base64 encoded payload that is encrypted using an XOR-based algorithm with the hardcoded key ***KJKLO***.
The SquirrelWaffle CnC responds with a Base64 encoded payload that uses the same encryption schema with another format that uses two tab characters as delimiter between fields.

actions.name: Download and execute second-stage payload
actions.description: Squirrelwaffle writes second-stage payload to a .txt file and executes it, leading to Cobalt Strike stager.

evidence.quote: This second-stage payload will be written to a filename that consists of eleven random alphanumeric characters appended with a .txt extension, and then executed by SquirrelWaffle.
This second-stage payload will be written to a filename that consists of eleven random alphanumeric characters appended with a .txt extension, and then executed by SquirrelWaffle.

actions.name: Deploy Cobalt Strike beacon
actions.description: Cobalt Strike stager downloads and decrypts Cobalt Strike beacon from C2 server.

evidence.quote: The Cobalt Strike stager sends an HTTPS GET request to 213.227.154[.]92 with the path /jquery-3.3.1.slim.min.js.
hxxps://systemmentorsec.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js,
The Cobalt Strike stager sends an HTTPS GET request to 213.227.154[.]92 with the path /jquery-3.3.1.slim.min.js.

The Cobalt Strike beacon observed by Zscaler ThreatLabz contains the following CnC servers:
*hxxps://systemmentorsec.com/jquery-3.3.1.min.js,*
*hxxps://213.227.154.92/jquery-3.3.1.min.js*
Once a victim clicks on the URL, a ZIP file is downloaded that contains a Microsoft Word document.
This document is using a DocuSign template lure that instructs the user to enable a macro to view the content
Once the user enables the macro, an *AutoOpen()* subroutine is called which then executes a malicious Visual Basic Application (VBA) macro.
The document that contains the macro code leverages cscript.exe to extract the embedded VBS file, which is written to the %ProgramData% folder, and executed using wscript.exe.
The payload DLL is executed via rundll32.exe by invoking the export function name *ldr*.

Once the malware decodes all of the CnC domains and IP addresses to block, it creates a **socket** and sends the data using the **send()** function and receives the content from the CnC using **recv()** calls.
The SquirrelWaffle CnC response may also contain a second-stage payload.

Zscaler ThreatLabz has observed Squirrelwaffle deliver an executable file with the MD5 hash 116301FD453397FDF3CB291341924147.
This file is packed and decrypted in memory to produce a Cobalt Strike stager with the MD5 hash 38DB72B33ABCEA250F5B7CB5AB514B2C, which further downloads the Cobalt Strike beacon.
